lines.trans: Hey there, it is me again.
I would like to know if you all accept a security deposit.
I will deposit up to six months.
I will deposit a year! I will pay during the year.
I will buy this house, just please let me live there!
I want to live in a place where I do not need to take the subway.
Just to get there and buy a bread roll.
Hey, please, do not hang up!
I am going to have to go back to my mother's house.

I would like to know if you all accept a security deposit.
I will deposit up to six months.

I will buy this house, just please let me live there!

Good afternoon!

meanings.note: Takes a direct object for payment methods or terms.

examples.trans: Do you all accept a deposit?
They do not accept delays.

meanings.note: Standard time unit; plural anos.

examples.trans: I will deposit a year!
She has been looking for three years.

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.

examples.trans: See you later!
See you later. Thanks!

meanings.note: Everyday adjective in tá bom (okay), boa tarde (good afternoon), and Bom, pessoal (Well, folks).

examples.trans: All right, I'll go.
Some numbers are good.

meanings.note: Means both a house building and home.

examples.trans: I will buy this house!

examples.text: Vou voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Used with a or para/pra for reaching a destination.

examples.text: Só pra chegar e comprar um pão.
examples.trans: Just to get there and buy a roll.
He arrived early today.

meanings.note: Everyday verb for purchasing goods or property.

examples.trans: I will buy this house!
I went to buy a bread roll.

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.

examples.trans: It’s a marketing meeting.
I’m in finance.

meanings.note: Deixa eu + infinitive is the natural spoken Brazilian frame for let me...

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.
examples.trans: Let me tell you something.
Leave your phone on the desk.

meanings.note: Used for putting down money or a security deposit.

examples.trans: I will deposit up to six months.
I will deposit a full year!

meanings.note: Security deposit or bank deposit.

examples.trans: Do you accept a deposit?
I made the deposit early today.

meanings.note: On a phone call, desligar means to hang up.

examples.text: Ei, por favor, não desliga, não!
examples.trans: Hey, please do not hang up!
He turned off his phone.

meanings.note: Indicates duration across a period of time.

examples.trans: I pay throughout the year.
He spoke during the meeting.

meanings.note: Coordinating conjunction pronounced [i] in natural Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Ela faltou e adiantou o trabalho.
examples.trans: She missed it and got ahead on her work.
There are good and bad numbers.

meanings.note: Used to call someone's attention urgently.

examples.text: Ei, por favor, não desliga, não!
examples.trans: Hey, please do not hang up!
Hey, wait a second!

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.

examples.trans: He is in the meeting.
She stays on her phone.

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
I’m not going.

meanings.note: In por favor, the standard polite 'please'.

examples.text: Ei, por favor, não desliga, não!
examples.trans: Hey, please do not hang up!
Can you do me a favor?

meanings.note: Conditional eu gostaria softens a refusal (I would like to, but...).

examples.trans: I would like to, but I have work.
I really like this team.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.

examples.trans: I’m going to the meeting.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Any location or neighborhood.

examples.trans: I want to live in a better place.
This place is very quiet.

meanings.note: First-person singular object clitic.

examples.trans: Would you help me real quick?

examples.text: Por favor, me deixa morar aqui!
examples.trans: Please let me live here!

meanings.note: Underground urban train system.

examples.trans: I do not need to take the subway.

examples.text: A estação de metrô fica perto.
examples.trans: The subway station is nearby.

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?
That is my job.

meanings.note: Takes the preposition em for the place where one lives.

examples.trans: I want to live in a better place.
She lives near here.

meanings.note: Female parent; plural mães.

examples.text: Meu pai e minha mãe me bloquearam.
examples.trans: My dad and my mom blocked me.

examples.text: Vou voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Calendar month; plural meses drops the circumflex.

examples.trans: I will deposit up to six months.

examples.text: Falta um mês para a viagem.
examples.trans: There is one month left until the trip.

meanings.note: In the phrase de novo, means 'again'.

examples.trans: Hey, it is me again.

examples.text: Na hora de botar de novo, impossível.
examples.trans: When it was time to put it back again, impossible.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.

examples.trans: No, I’m not going.
Aren’t you going?

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: What is your job title?
Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Friendly, upbeat Brazilian greeting or attention-getter.

examples.trans: Hey there, excuse me, my friend.
Hey there, it is me again.

meanings.note: Takes a direct object for the thing paid for.

examples.trans: I will pay during the year.
Who is going to pay for the coffee?

meanings.note: Used for taking transport, grabbing items, or taking an apartment first.

examples.trans: They will grab it ahead of me.
I do not need to take the subway.

meanings.note: Expresses duration (por uma hora) and fixed phrases like por exemplo.

examples.trans: I stayed there for an hour.
Look at her, for example.

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: I’m going to the meeting.
Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Takes de before a noun (precisa da ajuda) and links directly to an infinitive (precisava gritar).

examples.text: Ela precisa da ajuda do colega.
examples.trans: She needs her colleague's help.
Did you need to shout at me?

meanings.note: Singular um pão in Brazil usually means a French bread roll.

examples.text: Só pra chegar e comprar um pão.
examples.trans: Just to get there and buy a roll of bread.
I bought fresh bread in the morning.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.
What is this, man?

meanings.note: Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Is that what you want?

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.
Do you know the answer?

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Invariable cardinal number.

examples.trans: I will deposit up to six months.
The meeting starts at six.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.

examples.trans: I’m in finance.
It’s a marketing meeting.

meanings.note: Limits a statement (eu só quero) or forms só que (except that / the catch is).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

examples.text: Só que agora ela precisa de ajuda.
examples.trans: Except now she needs help.

meanings.note: Time between midday and evening; boa tarde! greets or bids farewell in the afternoon.

examples.trans: Good afternoon!

examples.text: A reunião é hoje à tarde.
examples.trans: The meeting is this afternoon.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?
There are some good numbers.

meanings.note: Plural addressee pronoun across Brazil, taking third-person plural verb forms.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you all look closely, there are numbers.
Are you all going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Used with para/pra for going back to a place.

examples.text: Vou ter que voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to have to go back to my mother's house.
He comes back tomorrow.
